newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Bancoquia to clean up past-due loans.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Bancoquia to clean up past-due loans.

text.p: Spain's Banco Santander SA is unlikely to see any profit this year from its takeover of Bancoquia, Colombia's eighth largest commercial bank in assets, a top bank official said.
Bancoquia changed its name to Banco Santander Colombia SA Thursday to reflect its imminent takeover by the Spanish banking giant.
Its president, Gabriel Jaramillo, cautioned in a Reuter interview late Thursday that 1997 will be something less than a banner year for the newly-named bank, however.
"We're clearly not going to have any profit this year because we're going to devote ourselves to building a platform for future expansion," Jaramillo said.

"Before that growth, we have to put our house in order," he added, saying the bank's plans, apart from a cutback in staff and an upgrading of its branch network, included a dramatic increase in loan-loss provisions.

As of March, Bancoquia's past-due loans totaled about $80 million and only 37 percent of them were backed by reserves, Jaramillo said. He said the bank's goal, in line with the strict standards of the Santander banking group, was to increase provisions to the point where they cover 100 percent of outstanding loans.

Jaramillo said he was unable to estimate what the bank's 1997 net profit would have been without the huge increase in loan-loss provisions. But its first quarter net totaled just $5.3 million against total assets of $1.4 billion and was down three percent from the same quarter last year.

Thursday's decision to change the Medellin-based bank's name followed last month's announcement of Banco Santander's purchase of a 55 percent stake in Bancoquia for $146 million. The deal is expected to be completed before July 30.
Colombia's Banking Association said last month that the number of bad loans in the country had increased dramatically.
Leasing companies were especially hard hit, it said, noting that there had been a 217 percent increase in foreclosures by such companies between March 1996 and 1997.

Banks experienced an 85.7 percent increase in bad loans during the same time period, the association said, adding that the problem underscored the need to slash domestic interest rates and cut some of the bureaucratic requirements for restructuring loans.
